terms: Bipolar Survey
Rating scale (e.g. minus 5 to plus 5) of qualities like cleanliness; used for environmental quality.
Choropleth Map
Map using graded colours to show variation by area; e.g. population density or income across regions.
Qualitative Data
Descriptive non-numerical: photographs, sketches, interviews; capture meaning and perception.
Quantitative Data
Numerical measurements: pebble size, river velocity, pedestrian counts; can be statistically analysed.
Sampling Methods
Random (e.g. dice), systematic (every nth), stratified (proportional by group); each suits different investigations.
Spearman's Rank
Statistical test of correlation between two ranked variables; values from minus 1 to plus 1.
Bid Rent Theory
Alonso's 1964 model: land value decreases with distance from CBD; can be tested with rateable values fieldwork.
Chi-Squared Test
Compares observed vs expected frequencies in categorical data; suitable for testing distribution patterns.
Ethical Considerations
Consent for questionnaires, anonymisation, environmental impact of sampling, BPS Code; risk assessment before fieldwork.
Hypothesis Formation
Testable prediction (e.g. 'pebble size decreases downstream'); needs null version for statistical testing.
Spearman's Rank
Non-parametric correlation test for ranked data; rs from minus 1 to plus 1; tested at 0.05 significance level.
Standard Deviation
Measure of spread around mean; 68% of normal distribution within 1 SD; used to compare variability.
Coastal Variety
UK's 17,820km coast includes rocky (Cornwall), chalk (Dover), sandy (East Anglia), estuarine (Severn).
Glaciation Legacy
Last Ice Age (until c.10,000 years ago) shaped uplands with U-shaped valleys, corries, ribbon lakes.
Lowland Britain
Southeast: younger, softer sedimentary rocks (chalk, clay); flatter relief; e.g. London Basin, East Anglia.
River Patterns
Major rivers (Thames, Severn, Trent) flow from uplands to lowlands; demonstrate upper, middle, lower course features.
Tees-Exe Line
Diagonal line dividing UK between upland west/north and lowland south/east; reflects geological boundary.
Upland Britain
Northwest and west: older, harder rocks (granite, slate); higher relief; e.g. Scottish Highlands, Lake District, Snowdonia.
Drought
Prolonged below-average rainfall; can be meteorological, agricultural or hydrological; East Africa 2011 famine, California 2012-17.
Hazard vs Disaster
Hazard is natural threat (volcano); disaster is realised damage to humans; risk depends on exposure and vulnerability.
Park's Disaster Response Curve
Stages following disaster: stable, deteriorating, search-rescue, relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction; varies by HIC/LIC.
Risk Equation
Risk = hazard frequency x population x vulnerability; reducing vulnerability through preparation cuts disaster impact.
Tropical Storms
Hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (Pacific), cyclones (Indian Ocean); form over 27 degrees C ocean; Saffir-Simpson scale 1-5.
Wildfires
Uncontrolled vegetation fires; intensified by climate change; Australia 2019-20 burnt 18 million hectares, killed 1 billion animals.
Circular Economy
Reduce-reuse-recycle replacing linear take-make-dispose; design for disassembly; Ellen MacArthur Foundation.
Critical Raw Materials
EU list of 30 materials essential to economy and supply-risky; includes rare earths, lithium, cobalt for green tech.
Lithium Triangle
Chile-Bolivia-Argentina contain 60% of world lithium reserves in salt flats; critical for EV batteries.
Peak Oil
Hubbert's 1956 theory of maximum extraction point; conventional peak debated; unconventional sources (shale) postponed.
Resource Curse
Paradox of resource-rich countries underperforming: Dutch Disease, corruption, conflict; e.g. DRC coltan, Niger oil.
Resource Frontier
Newly exploited regions: Arctic oil/gas, deep-sea mining; environmental risks balance against economic potential.
Demographic Transition Model
Five-stage model of birth/death rate as country develops; UK at Stage 4, Niger Stage 2, Japan Stage 5 (declining).
HDI
Human Development Index by UN: composite of life expectancy, education and GNI per capita; Norway 0.961, Niger 0.400.
HIC, NEE, LIC
World Bank categories: High-Income Country (UK, US), Newly Emerging Economy (India, Brazil), Low-Income Country (Mali, DRC).
India Development
NEE with 1.4 billion people; IT sector (Bangalore), TNCs like Tata; persistent inequality and rural poverty.
Rostow's Stages
1960 economic development model: traditional, preconditions, take-off, drive to maturity, mass consumption.
Top-down vs Bottom-up Aid
Top-down = large government projects (dams); bottom-up = small community schemes (e.g. WaterAid wells); latter more sustainable.

Carbon footprint
The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by a person, product or organisation, usually expressed in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.
Climate change consequences
Rising global temperatures bring sea-level rise, more extreme weather and shifting habitats, affecting people unevenly across the world.
Human impact on the environment
Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and intensive farming increase greenhouse gas emissions, pollute air and water, and degrade ecosystems.
Reduce, reuse, recycle
The waste hierarchy: cutting consumption first, then reusing items, then recycling materials, to reduce landfill and resource use.
Renewable energy
Energy from naturally replenished sources such as wind, solar and hydro power, which produce little or no carbon emissions in use.
Sustainable development
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

Tropical circulation: warm air rises at equator (low pressure, rainforests), descends at 30 degrees (high pressure, deserts).
ITCZ
Intertropical Convergence Zone where trade winds meet near equator; band of heavy convectional rainfall, migrates seasonally.
Microclimate
Local variation in climate over small area due to factors like aspect, urban heat island, water bodies or vegetation.

Constructive Plate Margin
Boundary where plates move apart and magma rises to create new crust; e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge produces Iceland's volcanism.
Destructive Plate Margin
Boundary where oceanic plate subducts beneath continental; produces composite volcanoes and megathrust earthquakes (e.g. Nazca-South American).

7.0 magnitude quake near Port-au-Prince killed around 220,000; example of LIC vulnerability with weak buildings and poor response.
Pyroclastic Flow
Fast-moving cloud of hot ash, gas and rock from explosive volcano; killed 30,000 at St Pierre, Martinique (Mt Pelee 1902).
Richter Scale
Logarithmic measure of earthquake magnitude based on seismic wave amplitude; each whole number is 10x larger amplitude.
Endogenous Factors
Internal characteristics shaping place: location, topography, demographics, land use, history; root identity.
Exogenous Factors
External relationships: migration, capital flows, government policy, tourism; constantly reshape places.
Gentrification
Ruth Glass's 1964 term for middle-class arrival in working-class areas; rising rents displace original residents; e.g. Hackney.
Placelessness
Edward Relph's 1976 term for homogenised landscapes lacking distinctive character; e.g. airport terminals, chain stores.
Rebranding
Place marketing changing image to attract investment, residents, tourists; e.g. Liverpool Capital of Culture 2008.
Sense of Place
Subjective meanings attached to location: insider/outsider, near/far perceptions; studied by humanistic geographers like Tuan.
Biotic and Abiotic
Biotic = living components (plants, animals, fungi); abiotic = non-living (water, soil, climate, light).
Deforestation in Amazon
Around 17% of Amazon lost since 1970s; causes include cattle ranching (80%), soy, logging, mining, road-building.
Food Web
Network of feeding relationships showing energy transfer: producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, decomposers.
Nutrient Cycle
Movement of nutrients between biomass, soil, litter; rainforests rely on rapid recycling due to poor soils.
Rainforest Stratification
Vertical layers: emergent (50m+), canopy (30-45m), under-canopy, shrub layer, forest floor; each with adapted species.
Sustainable Management
Use that meets present needs without compromising future; e.g. selective logging, ecotourism, FSC certification, debt-for-nature swaps.

Cutting the UK's carbon footprint
The UK aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through renewable energy, efficiency, transport changes and its legally binding net zero target.
Green belt
Land around cities protected from most development to limit urban sprawl, though it constrains where new homes can be built.
Greenfield vs brownfield
Greenfield sites are undeveloped land, often on city edges, while brownfield sites were previously built on; each has costs and benefits for housing.
Housing shortage
Demand for homes outstrips supply, especially in south-east England, raising prices and forcing difficult decisions about where to build.
UK energy mix
The combination of fossil fuels, nuclear and growing renewables used to supply the UK's energy, shifting over time to cut carbon emissions.
UK population growth
The UK population is growing and ageing, driven by natural change and migration, increasing demand for housing, services and infrastructure.

Employment structure
The share of workers in each sector; as countries develop, employment generally shifts from primary work towards tertiary and quaternary work.
Energy security
Having reliable, affordable energy supplies; countries improve it by diversifying sources, increasing domestic production and managing demand.
Informal sector
Unregulated, untaxed work such as street vending, common in LIC cities where formal jobs are scarce but incomes are still needed.
Non-renewable energy
Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — are finite stores of energy that release carbon dioxide when burned.

Movement of people from cities to smaller towns and rural areas, encouraged by commuting, remote working and perceived quality of life.
International Migration
Migration has increased the UK's population and diversity; migrants are often of working age, affecting the labour supply and services.
North-South Divide
Broad economic gap between the generally wealthier South East of England and many northern regions, visible in incomes, house prices and health.
Post-Industrial Economy
An economy dominated by services, finance, research and the knowledge sector after the decline of traditional manufacturing and heavy industry.
Soft Power
Influence gained through culture, media, diplomacy and education rather than force; the UK exerts it through the BBC, universities and the Commonwealth.
Favela Bairro Project
Rio scheme upgrading favelas: paved roads, sewers, schools; improved conditions for 250,000 people.
Lagos Nigeria
Africa's largest city (15 million); rapid growth, traffic gridlock; Eko Atlantic land-reclamation project responds.
Megacity
Urban area with 10 million+ inhabitants; over 33 worldwide; mostly in NICs (Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Sao Paulo).
Push and Pull Factors
Push: rural poverty, lack of jobs, drought; pull: employment, education, healthcare, services; drives rural-urban migration.
Rio de Janeiro
Brazilian megacity (13 million) with extreme inequality; wealthy beachside districts (Ipanema) and favelas like Rocinha.
Urbanisation
Increasing proportion of population living in cities; 56% globally in 2020, projected 68% by 2050.
